newsitem.title: USA: Artists and repertoire scouts discuss record industry woes.
newsitem.headline: Artists and repertoire scouts discuss record industry woes.

text.p: It may be one of the last few businesses on earth where you can go from a zero to a hero in a year.
That's the best part about signing new artists in the $12 billion record industry, according to Ron Fair, senior vice president of Artists & Repertoire (A&R) for Bertelsmann AG's RCA Records.
A&R executives are the people who scout and sign new talent within the record industry and bring them to the consumer, in hopes of selling millions of copies.

But Fair, a 16 year veteran who just signed the band Wild Orchid and many others like Natalie Cole, discussed at a recent panel the increasing pressures for A&R executives in the record industry as it goes through a painful maturation.

"Not to portray doom and gloom, but we're all living probably in the worst period for record retail stores in the history of the business as a business," Fair said, noting the closure of over 500 record stores in the past nine months at chains like Musicland Stores Corp and Wherehouse, which just emerged from bankruptcy.
Mark Kates, director of A&R for Seagram Co Ltd's Geffen Records, who was also at the panel sponsored by the Los Angeles Music Network (LAMN), agreed.
"It can't be emphasized enough...how brutal it is right now," said Kates, who brought hit artist Beck to Geffen and performed A&R duties for bands Nirvana and Hole.
Both executives said the ongoing contraction in the retail sector, which overexpanded too rapidly, has had a direct chilling effect on A&R decisions.

"We're in the middle of that (contraction) process now, so when you're signing new artists and launching new groups, the whole climate at retail has changed. They won't take as many albums of a new act without a given story," Fair said.
"It's a lot different, a lot tougher, you have to be a lot more calculated," he said, noting the retail "thing" is a daily reality.
The short attention span of both the audience and labels, who have jumped quickly from act to act in search of the big hit, have contributed to the industry's woes, they said.
"It takes a long time to break new acts. It's very very competitive out there," Fair said, noting the payoff was well worth it for labels who stuck with acts.
"Atlantic Records did it with Jewel, who did a year or so of touring with an acoustic guitar and a band before she became an MTV phenomenon and pop star," he said.
Both said they need autonomy to do their job, but the specter of dragging one's record company down with a bad decision is a constant reality check.

"Every investment a record company makes is triggered, directly or indirectly, by an A&R decision," said Tess Taylor, president of the Los Angeles Music Network and moderator of the panel discussion on March 26 on talent acquisition.
"Successful A&R decisions are vital for this industry's future health and welfare," she said.

"There are some times when you don't want a democratic analysis of something. You do it because of your own way of looking at it. But as it gets more competitive and difficult out there..you have to be completely convinced beyond a shadow of a doubt that it's there," Kates said.
He said he doesn't lie awake at night wondering how many Grammys his acts - like Beck - will win, but rather he worries about how his new acts will be received.

"You spend a lot more time thinking about and ultimately working on things that aren't successful than you do on things that are," he said. "Successful projects reach the public. Failure is omnipresent, and it's omnipresent in the record business, particularly at the moment," Kates said.
Fair said "the truth is I have total autonomy and zero autonomy." While he likes to go into a signing with his label backing him, he tries to stick with his own vision.
"At the base of every project there is a madman, there's somebody who puts their ass on the line," he said.
Kates sees a bright future for A&R executives as digital downloading of music to the consumer becomes commonplace.
"Even digital downloading is about content. Someone's still going to have find the content. Hopefully, technology is going to open up more channels to people," he said.
"By the time I'm 52, I'll be a character actor on TV," Fair half-joked, but then added there will always be viable categories to pursue in A&R.
"There are so many ways to appraoching it and they're all absolutely totally valid. There really is no rule book to this."
